lesson.title: Rebase a Feature Branch onto Main and Resolve Conflicts
lesson.goal: rebase a feature branch onto main with git and resolve the conflicts

sources.title: Rebase a Feature Branch onto Main and Resolve Conflicts

steps.title: Rebase a feature branch onto main
steps.instructions: In an empty folder run `git init -b main`, commit a file, create a feature branch with `git switch -c feature/login` and commit to it, then switch back to main and commit a change to a different file. Switch to the feature branch and run `git rebase main` so its commits are replayed on top of main without a merge commit.

targets.caption: The feature branch commits were replayed on top of main

explanations.topic: Rebasing gets main's commits into the feature branch without a merge commit
Commits are set aside and reapplied on the latest main commit
Why it's called rebasing: old base vs new base commit

hints: Make sure main has a commit the feature branch doesn't, and that it touches a different file.
Run the rebase from the feature branch: `git switch feature/login`, then `git rebase main`.
Check with `git log --oneline --graph --all`: the feature commit should sit above main's latest commit, with no merge commit.
common_mistakes: Running `git rebase main` while still on main, which does nothing.
Running `git merge main` instead of rebasing, which creates a merge commit.
Editing the same file on both branches, which causes a conflict this step doesn't cover.
Forgetting to commit on main before rebasing, so there is nothing new to rebase onto.
Using an older git where `git init -b` or `git switch` isn't supported.
steps.code:
git init -b main
git add . && git commit -m "initial commit"
git switch -c feature/login
git commit -am "add login"
git switch main
git commit -am "update readme"
git switch feature/login
git rebase main

steps.title: Check whether the branch was pushed
steps.instructions: Run `git branch -a` to list local and remote branches. Only rebase your feature branch if it does not appear under `remotes/`, because rebasing pushed commits rewrites their hashes.

targets.caption: Remote-tracking branches appear under remotes/. If your feature branch is listed there, don't rebase it.

explanations.topic: Golden rule: never rebase commits you've already pushed
Rebasing changes commit hashes, so local and remote history no longer match
git merge never rewrites history, so it keeps all commit hashes
Use git branch -a to check whether the feature branch was pushed

hints: The video uses a git branch flag that lists remote branches along with your local ones.
In the output, look for your feature branch under `remotes/` (e.g. `remotes/origin/<branch>`). Only rebase if it isn't there.
common_mistakes: Running plain `git branch`, which shows only local branches and hides remote ones.
Assuming the branch is safe to rebase without checking the `remotes/` entries.
Running the command outside the git repository, which fails with 'fatal: not a git repository'.
Trusting a stale list of remote branches. Run `git fetch` first if teammates may have pushed the branch.

steps.title: Start a conflicting rebase
steps.instructions: Give your feature branch three new commits whose 1st and 3rd change the same line of a file (e.g. login.txt) that new commits on main also change, with the 2nd editing a different file. Run `git rebase main`, then `git status` to see the rebase paused on the first commit with a conflict.

targets.caption: Rebase pauses on the first conflicting commit
git status confirms the rebase is still in progress
More feature commits are still to be reapplied

explanations.topic: Rebase sets your commits aside and reapplies them one by one, so each can conflict
Making main's latest commit the new base of the feature branch
A conflict pauses the rebase; git status shows which commit failed and what remains
Fixing rebase conflicts works like fixing merge conflicts

hints: Make sure you are on your feature branch, not main, before running the rebase.
Your setup needs main and the feature branch to both edit the same line of one file after they diverged, otherwise no conflict appears.
After the CONFLICT message, run `git status` to see 'rebase in progress' and the remaining commands.
If your branch rebased cleanly, reset it and add commits on both branches that change the same line of the same file.
common_mistakes: Running `git rebase main` while checked out on main instead of the feature branch.
Editing different lines on the two branches, so Git merges cleanly and no conflict appears.
Forgetting to commit the main-branch changes, so there is nothing to rebase onto.
Panicking at the conflict and running `git rebase --abort` before inspecting `git status`.

steps.title: Resolve conflict and continue rebase
steps.instructions: Open the conflicted file, remove the `<<<<<<<`, `=======` and `>>>>>>>` markers keeping the code that should stay, then `git add` it. Run `git rebase --continue` and in Vim press Esc then type `:wq` to keep the commit message.

targets.caption: Open the conflicted file and remove the conflict markers
Stage the fixed file, then continue the rebase

explanations.topic: git add marks the conflicted file as resolved
Leaving Vim with Esc and :wq keeps the commit message

hints: Open each conflicted file. Run git status to see which ones are listed as 'both modified'.
Delete every <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>> line. Keep only the code that should remain after the rebase.
Run git add on each fixed file, then run git rebase --continue (do not run git commit).
When Vim opens, press Esc, type :wq and press Enter to keep the commit message as it is.
common_mistakes: Leaving a conflict marker line in the file.
Running git rebase --continue before git add-ing the resolved file.
Running git commit instead of git rebase --continue.
Getting stuck in Vim by typing without pressing Esc first, or forgetting the colon in :wq.

steps.title: Fix final conflict and finish
steps.instructions: Resolve the remaining conflict the same way, `git add` the file and run `git rebase --continue` again. Then run `git status` and `git log --oneline --graph` to confirm a clean, linear history on top of main.

precision_checks.label: No rebase in progress
precision_checks.command: test ! -d "$(git rev-parse --git-path rebase-merge)" && test ! -d "$(git rev-parse --git-path rebase-apply)"

targets.caption: Git confirms the rebase completed after the last commit
git status no longer reports a rebase in progress

explanations.topic: Non-conflicting commits are applied automatically during rebase
Rebase pauses again at each conflicting commit
Using git status to confirm you are out of the rebasing state

hints: The third commit conflicts just like the first one did, so resolve it the same way.
Open the conflicted file, keep the content you want and delete every <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>> line.
Stage the fixed file with `git add <file>`, then run `git rebase --continue` and save/close the commit message editor.
Run `git status`. It should say 'On branch ...' with no 'currently rebasing' note. `git log --oneline --graph` should show a straight line on top of main.
common_mistakes: Leaving conflict markers in the file before running git add.
Running `git commit` instead of `git rebase --continue`.
Forgetting to stage the resolved file, so `git rebase --continue` refuses to proceed.
Not closing the editor (e.g. not running :wq in Vim), so the rebase appears stuck.
Assuming the rebase is done after the second commit even though git status still shows a rebase in progress.
steps.code:
git add <conflicted-file>
git rebase --continue
git status
